chapter_theme: Akananuru 21 to 40, in the anthology's fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems of men on the road to wealth arguing with their hearts and women counting seasons, set beside hill courtships at the millet field, marutham quarrels settled by a child or sharpened by gossip, mullai camps and homecomings, and neythal evenings. Puram fame (Alankanam, Thithiyan, Kari's Pennai, Korkai, Kolli) supplies the similes for private feeling.

21.reading: Halfway across a waterless forest, the man rebukes his heart, which now wants to turn back: it was the heart that refused his plea not to leave the girl with jasmine-bud teeth and settled on the venture, so it must rise at once and help bring home wealth that will make the house glad.
21.nuance: The roles are reversed from the usual quarrel: the man had argued for staying, the heart for going, and now he holds the heart to its own choice. The goal is named as மனைநக, that the house may laugh, so the journey is cast as a gift to the home rather than flight from it.

thinai_evidence.note: a man already on the road for wealth argues against return

comparisons.vehicle: மனைஇள நொச்சி மௌவல் வால்முகைத் துணை நிரைத்தன்ன
comparisons.tenor: her white teeth, as a paired row of jasmine buds on the young nochi of the house

occasion.words: இடைச் சுரத்து நின்று மீளலுற்ற நெஞ்சினைக் கழறியது

iraicchi.act: the male wild dog attacks a boar because his mate, weak after whelping, is hungry
iraicchi.sense: the road itself shows a male who fights to feed the mate he provides for, the very task the heart has abandoned halfway

colophon.thurai: பொருள் வலிக்கப்பட்டுப் பிரிந்த தலைமகன் இடைச் சுரத்து நின்று மீளலுற்ற நெஞ்சினைக் கழறியது.

22.reading: The girl recalls the midnight rite her mother held to cure her: old women said Murugan's power had seized her, the velan sacrificed and scattered red millet with blood, and in that very night her lover slipped past the house guards like a hunting tiger, so that in his embrace she laughed at an offering wasted on a stranger priest while the true cure of her sickness had come.
22.nuance: She speaks to defend the man her friend has just blamed, and the defence is a confession: he risked the guarded house on the night of the rite. Her laughter judges the rite only as a diagnosis; it does not deny the god, whose fierce presence (அணங்கு, உருகெழு) the poem keeps.

thinai_evidence.note: a secret night meeting in the hill country

comparisons.vehicle: களிற்று - இரை தெரீஇய பார்வல் ஒதுக்கின் ஒளித்து இயங்கும் மரபின் வயப்புலி
comparisons.tenor: the lover slipping unseen past the house guards

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the friend has blamed the hero (இயற்பழிப்ப); the heroine answers in his praise

colophon.thurai: (1) வரைவிடை வைத்துப் பிரிந்த காலத்துத் தலைமகள் ஆற்றாளாகத் தோழி தலைமகனை இயற்பழிப்பத் தலைமகள் இயற்பட மொழிந்தது.

23.reading: The rains have spent themselves, the forest is fragrant with opening jasmine and pidavam, and in the hollows the stag, done grazing, embraces his doe, drinks the cool water and lies down; the woman asks her friend whether this is the time her man meant when he pointed to the jasmine on the house's nochi and said he would return by then from the wealth he went to earn.
23.nuance: The token he chose, the jasmine around the house's own hedge, now blooms on time, so his sign testifies against him. The poem never says he is late; it lets the season and the stag say it.

thinai_evidence.note: forest at the end of the rains, a woman waiting on a promised season

comparisons.tenor: the young kodal shoots in the hollows, like broken pieces of conch

iraicchi.act: the stag, done with grazing, embraces his loving doe, drinks with her and rests beside her
iraicchi.sense: the season has brought even the stag to his mate's side, which is where the man who named this season should now be

24.reading: At the end of the cold rains, when pakanrai buds open in the drizzle and the north wind hides the dawn, the man says his bright-browed wife swims alone through the long cold nights in her own town, while he is in the camp of a fierce king where elephants with tusks blunted on fort gates jangle their bells, drums roar at midnight and soldiers with unsheathed swords never sleep.
24.nuance: யாமே answers தம்ஊரோளே: the two halves weigh her sleepless night at home against the camp's sleepless night, so neither of them sleeps. The conch-cutter's discarded rings in the first simile are bangles, the wife's own ornament, set among the season's flowers.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainy season's end, and a wife who endures the waiting

comparisons.vehicle: வேளாப் பார்ப்பான் வாளரந் துமித்த வளைகளைந்து ஒழிந்த கொழுந்தின் அன்ன
comparisons.tenor: the closed pakanrai buds, like the waste curls left when the conch-cutter saws bangles
the dark clouds drifting across the wide sky, as if the sky were peeling

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; he speaks from the king's war camp

25.reading: Seeing her weep that spring, with its sandbanks of kaanji pollen and its cuckoos calling in turn, is surely the sign her man set for his return, her friend promises that he who crossed the hills whose falls sound like the music of Thithiyan, lord of Pothiyil, will come quickly with soft words of sorrow for her tears.
25.nuance: The friend puts apology into the absent man's mouth before he has come (நோவல், குறுமகள்), so her comfort is a script for his return. The spring is described as a season that even scorners cannot scorn, which makes his absence from it harder to excuse.

thinai_evidence.note: spring, and a man gone across the wild hills

comparisons.tenor: the cuckoo's calls in turn, as if it were speaking
the fine kongu pollen on the red ilavam, like gold poured into a coral casket
the falls on the hill, sounding like the sweet instruments of Thithiyan

26.reading: The wife asks her friend how she could sulk with her husband: once he praised her breasts and would not stop embracing, but lately he held back for fear of spilling the milk meant for their son, so she turned to the boy in the nurse's arms saying he suits the good women and she suits the son, and at that he said he too loved the child, held her from behind and wept, melting like ploughed red earth in the rain.
26.nuance: The child decides the quarrel twice: he is her reason to withdraw and the man's way back to her. The rain-on-ploughed-field simile gives the melting to him, so her question (புலத்தல் கூடுமோ) means that his tears have left her no ground for sulking.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife's sulking with a husband of the watered fields

comparisons.tenor: the white-stemmed mulli flowers, like fish bones

comparisons.vehicle: பெருங் கதவு பொருத யானை மருப்பின் இரும்புசெய் தொடியின் ஏர
comparisons.tenor: her breasts, like the iron rings on the tusk of an elephant that batters great gates

comparisons.vehicle: உறுபெயல் தண்துளிக்கு ஏற்ற பலஉழு செஞ்செய் மண்போல்
comparisons.tenor: the husband melting, like many-ploughed red earth taking the cool rain

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: after the hero, refused by the friend, came in by his own distress and was reconciled

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் தோழியை வாயில் வேண்டி அவளால் தான் வாயில் பெறாது ஆற்றாமையே வாயிலாகப் புக்குக் கூடிய தலைமகனீக்கத்துக்கண் புக்க தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

27.reading: The friend tells the girl, who has paled on hearing that her man will leave to fetch wealth across the tiger's forest, that she is naive: even if her red mouth with teeth like the pearls of Korkai does not hold him, how could her eyes, which outdo the blue lily and fight like a victorious spear swinging with blood, let him go?
27.nuance: The friend argues from the girl's own beauty, which is a comfort and a reproach at once: her body should be his reason to stay. The pearl simile carries a whole Pandya world (the Venkatam elephant, Korkai guarded by aram) into a two-line image of her teeth.

thinai_evidence.note: news of a departure for wealth across the wild forest

comparisons.tenor: her shining teeth, like the pearls of Korkai's great harbour
her red-streaked, fighting eyes, like a victorious spear swinging with blood

28.reading: With the man listening nearby, the friend warns the girl that the millet ears are bowing and harvested stalks are showing in the fields: if she, content with her hunter, does not rise and scare the parrots, her mother will say she cannot guard the crop and send others, and then his broad chest will be hard to reach.
28.nuance: The warning is meant for the overhearing man: the ripening millet dates the end of the field meetings, so he must turn the secret love into marriage before the harvest closes it.

thinai_evidence.note: a millet field guarded by a hill girl, and a hunter lover

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon adds that the overhearing is by day (பகலே சிறைப்புறம்)

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி சொல்லியது. இது, பகலே சிறைப்புறம்.

29.reading: Back from his work, the man answers his wife, who asks with a fading smile whether he forgot her: he left vowing that a day without thinking of her eyes would not be worth living, and in the burning waste where elephants chase mirages and wilt like boats in dried water, only his body stayed there, bound by shame to finish the task, while his foolish heart was always with her.
29.nuance: He splits himself to answer the charge: the body (உடம்பு) was held by நாண், the shame of an unfinished task, and the heart (நெஞ்சம்) never left. The tiger that will not eat prey fallen on its left side measures his resolve by a hunter's code of honour.

thinai_evidence.note: the separation recalled through the burning wasteland

comparisons.tenor: his unflinching heart, surpassing the tiger that will not eat an elephant fallen on its left
her eyes, like the two halves of a tender mango cut by a blade
the elephant wilting by the dry path, like a boat left where the water has gone

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீண்ட தலைமகன் எம்மையும் நினைத்தறிதிரோ? என்ற தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

30.reading: The friend tells the lord of a shore where fishermen haul in their catch together like ploughmen at a threshing floor, fling fish to fill the empty pots of those who beg, and sleep on the high dunes, that greatness is not lost by coming one day to the cool punnai grove and asking how she fares, and implies that to ask once and leave is no greatness.
30.nuance: The two closing lines can be read as a plea (would your greatness suffer if you came and asked?) or as a reproach (is it greatness to come once, ask, and go?); the generosity of his own fishermen is set before him as a standard either way.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen, the punnai grove and the lord of the shore

comparisons.vehicle: உமணர் அருந்துறை போக்கும் ஒழுகை நோன்பகடு ஒப்ப
comparisons.tenor: the fishermen straining at the net together, like the strong oxen of the salt-traders' carts
the fishermen gathering their catch, like ploughmen heaping a great threshing floor
the punnai buds, unwashed pearls

iraicchi.act: the fishermen share their catch freely, filling the empty vessels of those who beg
iraicchi.sense: the lord of a shore whose people give so freely should not withhold from her the small gift of his concern, and with it the promise of marriage

31.reading: Hearing it said that she cannot bear the parting, the woman tells her friend of the road her man took: a season of failed rain when the fiery sun scorched the land, where bowmen of the rock forts shoot travellers whose eyes the vultures pluck, beyond which lie the many hills of the land of changed speech, outside the rule of the three Tamil kings.
31.nuance: The road ends at the border of the language: the measure of his distance is where Tamil stops being spoken (மொழிபெயர் தேஎத்த). The sense of 'சென்றார்' என்பு இலர் is unclear to me, and the colophon thurai breaks off before naming the speaker.

thinai_evidence.note: scorched land in a season of failed rain

comparisons.tenor: the sun's disc, red as fire
the blood streaming from the wounds, like an oleander garland laid out

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon thurai is cut off; speaker and addressee are inferred from the poem's தோழி

32.reading: She tells her friend how yesterday a jewelled man, looking like a patron but pleading like a suppliant, came to the millet field, called her a hill goddess who had stricken him and held her from behind; melting inside but afraid he would see it, she broke free like a startled doe and stood firm, and he went off like an elephant parted from its herd, so now she proposes they go and laugh at the gracious man who keeps trying, not knowing her shoulders are his alone.
32.nuance: Puram's pair of giver and receiver (புரவலன், இரவல்) is turned inside out: the man who looks like a patron begs. The plan to laugh at him is an assent in disguise, since in the same breath she says the claim to her shoulders is his.

thinai_evidence.note: a first meeting and embrace at the millet field

comparisons.tenor: the man's bearing, like a patron's
his humble words, like a suppliant's
the girl standing, like the goddesses of the hill
her melting inside, like earth under pouring rain
her breaking free, like a startled doe
the man going off, like an elephant parted from its herd

colophon.thurai: (1) பின்னின்ற தலைமகற்குக் குறை நேர்ந்த தோழிதலைமகட்குக் குறைநயப்பக் கூறியது. (2) தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொற்றதூஉமாம்.

33.reading: On the road the man tells his heart, which wants to turn back: it chose to leave the virtuous wife and to cross the land where a kite calls its mate, and now, halfway over the gravel hills, it would be better never to have parted from her with shoulders like the bamboo of Vanavan's Kolli; but to break off the work now would only win the laughter of others.
33.nuance: The poem does not deny the heart's longing; it concedes that never leaving would have been good (நன்றுமற் றில்ல) and then argues that turning back now is worse. Shame before others (பிறர்நகு) is the last argument, not wealth.

thinai_evidence.note: a man mid-journey, torn over the parting

comparisons.tenor: her curved, swelling shoulders, like the slender bamboo on Kolli

iraicchi.act: the male kite on the bare yaa tree keeps calling his hooked-beaked mate to come to him
iraicchi.sense: even the kite on this dry road calls its mate to its side, while the man has left his wife and may not even turn back to her

34.reading: His task done, the man urges his charioteer to hurry through the cool scrub where a stag feeds tender grass to his young doe and guards her while she sleeps, so that his heart may find ease with his shy wife, who in the house where swans play with their mates holds a parrot on her wrist and softly teaches it to say 'tell me he comes today', afraid the household will hear.
34.nuance: Both partners speak through creatures: his longing is shown in the stag's care, hers in the words she teaches the parrot because she is too shy to say them aloud.

thinai_evidence.note: scrubland in flower and a homecoming

comparisons.tenor: the white-topped pidavam bushes, flowering like garlands
the stag's twisted horns, like the forked stick a hunter carries
the pure-white swans, like the washerwoman's washed cloth left at the ford

iraicchi.act: the stag feeds tender grass to his young doe and guards her back while she sleeps
iraicchi.sense: the stag's care is the care the man is hurrying home to give his wife

35.reading: A mother whose daughter has run off with a man prays: the girl, forgetting those who bore and raised her, left the high-walled house desolate and dared the flesh-smelling road where bowmen honour hero-stones with peacock feathers, drums and toddy; may the stranger who became her companion in an unknown land adorn her again and again and put her to sleep on his chest, her curled hair like the fine ripples of Kari's Pennai river.
35.nuance: The prayer hands the stranger her own office: அணிந்து அணிந்து, adorning again and again, is what a mother does. The road is marked by offerings to the dead, so the daughter's path into marriage is drawn through a landscape of graves.

thinai_evidence.note: a daughter's flight with her lover across the wild road

comparisons.tenor: the daughter's curled dark hair, like the fine sand-ripples of the Pennai

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the deity she prays to

36.reading: The wife tells her husband, lord of a town where a great striped varal fish swallows the hook, tears the water-lily leaves, crushes the blue lilies, tangles the vallai creeper and will not come to the angler's pull, raging like a roped bull as it churns the pond each day, that the gossip of his wedding with a young girl in the marutham grove on the Vaigai's sands is louder than the shout of Chezhiyan's warriors on the day he crushed seven kings at Alankanam.
36.nuance: The gossip is measured by the most famous victory shout the audience knew, so a private wrong is given the volume of a public war. The fish's scene is the wife's hidden charge; the battle simile is her open one.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's union with another woman, and the wife's sulking

comparisons.tenor: the fish raging against the line, like an angry bull held by a rope
the gossip about the wedding, louder than the victory shout at Alankanam

occasion.words: பரத்தையிற் பிரிந்து வந்த தலைமகனோடு புலந்து சொல்லியது

ullurai.tenor: the husband and his new women

pairs.situation: he has swallowed the bait of a new woman
he spoils many women in his pleasure
no one can draw him back home
every day his affairs stir up the town

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses a fish of her own town's pond, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

colophon.thurai: தலைமகள் பரத்தையிற் பிரிந்து வந்த தலைமகனோடு புலந்து சொல்லியது.

37.reading: Breaking down under her friend's reassurance, the woman says that even if he has not forgotten her, this is the lovely spring: farmers thresh all night under dust like mist, rise at dawn to pluck mangoes green as parrots, drink new brew from leaf cups like oxen at a pond, eat horsegram and lentil porridge with milk, and rest at noon with their oxen in the marutham shade, a sweet season only for those who have partners to enjoy.
37.nuance: The farmers' full day, from night threshing to noon's rest with the oxen, is a picture of shared life; only the last line turns the whole landscape into her lack.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman without her partner in the spring

comparisons.tenor: the threshing dust, like a misty sky hiding the quarters
the green mangoes, like parrots
the farmers drinking deep, like oxen plunging into a pond
the white porridge, like drawn rods of silver

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee, the friend who gave the reassurance, is inferred

38.reading: The friend imagines the hill-man, garlanded with vengai and blue lily, bow in hand, coming to the old meeting places and finding the swing on the ashoka abandoned, the pool where lilies open like eyes, and the harvested millet field, and wonders whether he will turn back grieving, since she forgot to tell him that their village is the one on the high hill crowned by the white waterfall.
38.nuance: 'I forgot to tell him our village' is the real message for the overhearing man: the field trysts are over, and the way to her now runs through the village, that is, through marriage. Line 15 (ஐ.தேங்கு) looks corrupt.

thinai_evidence.note: hill flowers, a harvested millet field and the hill-man

comparisons.tenor: the long-petalled blue lilies of the pool, opening like eyes

occasion.words: பகலே சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்

colophon.thurai: (1) தோழி தலைமகன் குறைகூறியது. (2) பகலே சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியதூஉமாம். (3) தோழி குறிபெயர்த்திட்டுச் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

39.reading: The returned man tells his wife not to speak like a stranger, asking whether he ever thought of her: in a vast forest swept by a wildfire from rubbing bamboo, where travellers lost the path and elephants fled a tiger, he lay at sunset thinking of her and dreamed he found her brooding with loose bangles, stroked her brow and smoothed her hair asking why she sulked, and the false dream left him with empty hands; it is she who has not cared for his distress.
39.nuance: He turns her charge round: her sulk is answered by his dream of answering her sulk, so the dispute is already rehearsed in the dream, and the empty hand he woke to is his evidence that he thought of her.

thinai_evidence.note: a wildfire across the great forest on the road

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the record has no colophon thurai; speaker and situation are inferred from the poem (the returned man answers her complaint)

40.reading: At evening on the shore, as the backwater flowers close, the sea roars and herons crowd into the punnai nests, the woman tells her friend that though her man has gone without pity and left her heart in grief, may his friendship never break, and may her heart, which went to his breast of sweet sleep, not tire of staying there for want of kindness and come back.
40.nuance: She blesses the bond in the same breath as she names its cruelty. The heron that flees the reapers' drum to roost in the palmyra's inner frond is the picture of her own heart, which fled the evening's pain to his breast.

thinai_evidence.note: the seashore at evening

comparisons.tenor: the heron's cry, like the horn blown at the sluice

ullurai.tenor: the woman's heart and her absent husband

pairs.situation: her heart is frightened by the evening's pain
her heart has gone to rest on his breast

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses a heron of her husband's shore, near her own home and known to her (porul 7.26)

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்துழிக் கிழத்தி தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

links.note: Both are a man mid-road rebuking his heart for wanting to turn back; 21 holds the heart to its own choice and names the aim as making the house glad (மனைநக), 33 concedes never leaving would have been better and names the penalty as others' laughter (பிறர்நகு).
links.teaches: Read together they show the mid-road speech as a set argument with two stakes, the household's joy if he finishes and public ridicule if he quits, both expressed through laughter.

links.note: Kural 467 says to think before resolving and calls rethinking after resolve a lapse; in Akananuru 33 the man tells his heart it did not think then, and that to halt the work now would make him a thing others laugh at.
links.teaches: The poem shows the Kural's rule against second thoughts applied by a lover to his own heart, and adds what the maxim omits: the resolved deed costs a wife left behind, and the man accepts that cost rather than the shame of turning back.

links.note: 23 is the wife at the end of the rains, seeing the promised season come without him; 24 is a man in the king's camp at the end of the cold rains, picturing his wife alone through the nights.
links.teaches: Set side by side in the anthology's order, the same season is seen from the empty house and from the sleepless camp, so each poem supplies the half of the separation the other cannot see.

links.note: Both describe the king's war camp at midnight with the long-tongued bright bell (நெடுநா ஒண்மணி) and the roaring drum; Mullaippattu's king lies awake thinking of the enemy while his queen waits, and Akananuru 24's soldier speaks of his wife alone at home.
links.teaches: The shared bell formula shows the midnight camp was a stock scene, and the two poems use it from different ranks: the idyll gives it to the king, the short poem to a man in his army whose wife waits like the idyll's queen.

links.note: Kural 1268 has a man serving in the king's war wish the king victory so that he may feast at home with his wife by evening; Akananuru 24 is such a man in the king's camp at the end of the rains, measuring the camp's sleepless night against his wife's lonely one.
links.teaches: The couplet states the soldier-husband's wish as a sentence; the poem gives the night that produces it, the blunted tusks, the drums and the cold rain, so the Kural's two clauses read as the end of a long vigil.

links.note: In 25 the falls on the hill sound like the sweet music of Thithiyan, lord of Pothiyil, victor in battle; in 36 Thithiyan is one of the seven kings crushed by Chezhiyan at Alankanam.
links.teaches: One chief serves in adjacent akam poems as a figure of glory and as one of the defeated, which shows the poets drew on a chief's fame and his fall alike as material for similes.

links.note: Both tell Nedunchezhiyan's one-man victory over seven kings at Alankanam in the same phrase, எழுவர் நல்வலம் அடங்க; Purananuru 76 praises it as unheard of, Akananuru 36 uses its victory shout to measure the noise of gossip about a husband's new wife.
links.teaches: The identical phrase in a praise poem and in a wife's complaint shows the battle had a fixed formula that akam poets lifted whole, so a private quarrel could borrow the loudest public event the audience knew.

links.note: Both show hero-stones by a stony cairn (பதுக்கை) crowned with peacock feathers (பீலி சூட்டி) for men who died over cattle; Purananuru 264 is the lament for one such fallen man, Akananuru 35 sees such stones only as worship on the road a runaway daughter took.
links.teaches: The puram poem tells who lies under the stone and who will miss him; the akam poem shows how the same stones looked to a mother who saw only their danger, so a hero's memorial became a mark of the perils of the wild road.

links.note: Purananuru 126 praises Malaiyaman Kari as lord of the Pennai country and giver to bards; Akananuru 35 likens a daughter's hair to the fine sand-ripples of the Pennai at Kari's ford.
links.teaches: A patron's river, praised in puram for the gifts it brings bards, became in akam a stock likeness of a girl's beauty, so a chief's fame lent its landscape to love poetry.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai lists the velan's frenzy-ground (வேலன் தைஇய வெறியயர் களனும்) among Murugan's abodes, with red millet and blood scattered and the god called down (முருகாற்றுப் படுத்த), where seekers gain what they ask; Akananuru 22 describes the same rite and the heroine laughs that it was wasted on a stranger priest, since her lover was the cure.
links.teaches: The devotional idyll and the love poem share the rite's very words, but the akam poem limits its power: the god may come, yet the velan's diagnosis of a girl's sickness is wrong, so the rite's authority stops where secret love begins.

links.note: Kural 1323 asks whether any heaven equals sulking with one joined to you as water to earth; in Akananuru 26 the wife cannot sulk because her husband melted like ploughed red earth taking the rain.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the earth-and-water bond the reason sulking is sweet, while the poem uses the same image to end the sulk, which shows the likeness can either sustain lovers' quarrel or dissolve it, depending on who is melting.

links.note: In both a man back from the road answers his wife's charge that he forgot her: 29 says his body was held by shame to the work while his heart stayed with her, 39 offers a dream on the road in which he comforted her.
links.teaches: Two poets give the same answer in two forms, a division of body from heart and a dream, which shows that the reply to 'did you think of us' had to prove an inner presence the separation itself denied.
